children.title: Trump DOJ Orders Review of FBI Personnel Tied to January 6 Cases Before Patel Takes Office
children.description_short: On Jan. 31, 2025, DOJ ordered a review of personnel tied to Jan. 6 cases, before Kash Patel became FBI director.
children.description_medium: On January 31, 2025, Reuters reported that acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove directed federal prosecutors to list employees who worked on the January 6 Capitol investigation, while FBI officials tied to those cases faced personnel actions. The report described Patel as the nominee to lead the FBI, not its director. It does not substantiate a claim that Patel fired hundreds of agents for disloyalty.
children.description_long: On January 31, 2025, the Trump administration began a round of Justice Department and FBI personnel actions focused in part on staff who had worked on investigations related to the January 6 attack. Reuters reported that acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove told federal prosecutors to compile a list of prosecutors and FBI agents who participated in the Capitol investigation. The same report said a memo ordered eight FBI officials to resign or face dismissal because of their work on January 6 cases, and separately described about 20 probationary prosecutors fired under a Bove order. Reuters also reported that the FBI Agents Association warned potentially hundreds of agents could be affected; that was a warning about possible scale, not a reported count of agents already fired. Kash Patel was still the nominee to direct the bureau and had appeared at a confirmation hearing the day before. This episode therefore belongs to Trump administration and Justice Department actions before Patel became FBI director. The reporting supports a personnel review and identified removals, but does not establish that Patel fired hundreds of agents for insufficient loyalty.

children.title: FBI Forces Out at Least Three Senior Officials, Including Brian Driscoll
children.description_short: The FBI forced out at least three senior officials in August 2025, including former acting director Brian Driscoll.
children.description_medium: The Washington Post reported that the FBI forced out at least three senior officials during a period of conflict with the Trump administration. One was former acting director Brian Driscoll, who had resisted demands to identify agents involved in January 6 investigations. The report places these departures during Kash Patel’s tenure, but does not say every official was dismissed for the same reason.
children.description_long: On August 7, 2025, The Washington Post reported that the FBI had forced out at least three senior officials who had clashed with the Trump administration. One was Brian Driscoll, the bureau’s former acting director during the first weeks of Trump’s second term. The report said Driscoll was fired by senior leaders and would finish his last day on Friday, August 8; the people quoted said he was given no reason for the firing. During his brief time leading the bureau, Driscoll had resisted demands from Trump Justice Department appointees to identify agents who worked on January 6 investigations. The article said he later provided the department a list of more than 5,000 FBI personnel identified only by employee identification number. It placed the departures during Kash Patel’s tenure. This is a distinct August personnel episode from the January 2025 review and the February 2026 agent dismissals. The source does not establish that all three officials worked on January 6 cases, that the same decisionmaker fired each one, or that a formal written rationale was issued. It documents reported departures amid a wider dispute over the treatment of bureau personnel.

children.title: FBI Fires at Least a Dozen Agents Tied to Trump Classified-Documents Probe
children.description_short: The FBI fired at least a dozen staff tied to Trump’s classified-documents probe in February 2026, The Washington Post reported.
children.description_medium: On February 26, 2026, The Washington Post reported that FBI Director Kash Patel had fired at least a dozen agents and staff across the country who were tied to the probe into Donald Trump’s alleged mishandling of classified documents after he left office in 2021. This is a separate Patel-era episode; the report does not support the original claim that hundreds were fired for insufficient loyalty.
children.description_long: On February 26, 2026, The Washington Post reported that FBI Director Kash Patel had fired at least a dozen agents and staff across the country during that week. The article connected those employees to the FBI probe into Donald Trump’s alleged mishandling of classified documents after leaving office in 2021. It described the dismissals as a continuation of Patel’s purge of bureau employees. This is a separate, later episode from the January 2025 review directed by acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove and the August 2025 departures of senior FBI officials. The available report supports the number “at least a dozen” for this specific week and describes the employees as tied to the classified-documents investigation. It does not establish that hundreds of agents were dismissed, that every affected employee was deemed insufficiently loyal, or that the February 2026 dismissals included employees tied to the separate 2020-election investigation. The original combined entry blended these episodes and attributed the January review to Patel before he led the bureau. This card preserves the Washington Post’s reported connection and allegation wording without turning the report into an independent finding about each employee or the president.

title: Iran Nuclear Talks Had No Resumption Date as of July 14, 2025
description_short: Iranian officials said July 14, 2025, that no date or location had been set to resume U.S.-Iran nuclear talks after the June conflict.
description_medium: On July 14, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said no date or location had been set for resumed U.S.-Iran nuclear talks when asked about a possible meeting between Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff. Reuters had reported on July 1 that G7 foreign ministers urged negotiations to resume after the Iran-Israel ceasefire. These reports support an unscheduled diplomatic process, not Trump’s repeated promise of an imminent “historic, perfect” deal or a definitive collapse by July’s end.
description_long: On July 14, 2025, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said there was no date or location set to resume U.S.-Iran nuclear talks when asked whether Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi would meet with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff. The status followed the June ceasefire between Israel and Iran. On July 1, Reuters reported that Group of Seven foreign ministers had urged negotiations to resume for an agreement addressing Iran’s nuclear program. The same Reuters report said the United States and Iran had held talks since April and quoted Witkoff describing them as “promising,” while Washington hoped for a long-term peace deal. These sources trace the diplomatic context but do not establish that Trump repeatedly promised in July that a “historic, perfect” agreement was imminent. Nor do they show negotiations completely collapsed by July 31. The supported event is narrower: talks were unscheduled as of July 14 after a June conflict and a G7 appeal to resume negotiations. This evidence does not establish that a particular public statement damaged U.S. credibility, and the frozen entry’s causal judgment is not carried into this corrected copy. The reporting also does not establish that Iranian officials denied all serious talks were taking place.

title: Pam Bondi DOJ Drops All Pending Cases Against Trump Allies on Day One
blockers: The date and actor in the frozen record conflict with the accessed confirmation report: the Senate confirmed Bondi on February 4, 2025, so she was not Attorney General on January 20 and could not have ordered the claimed action as Attorney General that day.

No accessed source supports the broader allegation that Bondi directed dismissal of all pending federal cases against Trump allies on January 20. The closest documented action is President Trump’s January 20 clemency proclamation, which addressed January 6-related convictions and directed dismissal of pending indictments for conduct related to the Capitol events; it is a different actor and a narrower category than all cases against Trump associates.

The supplied counterpart entry-6611 repeats the day-one Bondi allegation with different case categories. Entry-6788 separately alleges a February motion to vacate all January 6 convictions and explicitly distinguishes it from Trump’s January 20 clemency order. Neither is a confirmed survivor, so this record cannot be converted into a duplicate merge or a second card about the proclamation.

title: USDA’s July 2025 PRWORA Notice Includes WIC, With State Implementation Varying
description_short: USDA’s July 10 notice listed WIC among food programs treated as federal public benefits; it did not announce the frozen record’s claimed February nationwide ban.
description_medium: On July 10, 2025, USDA published a notice interpreting PRWORA’s federal-public-benefit definition and listing WIC among the Food and Nutrition Service’s programs. USDA said it was still evaluating how to verify compliance and would issue later guidance. The notice supports a July agency interpretation, not a February blanket exclusion of lawful immigrant families. A contemporaneous NILC analysis said states could choose whether to offer or restrict WIC; it reported Idaho was the only state restricting federally funded WIC that month.
description_long: On July 10, 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture published a Federal Register notice interpreting how the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act applies to programs it administers. The notice said all 16 Food and Nutrition Service food programs meet the law’s federal-public-benefit definition and listed the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC). USDA also said it was still evaluating how it would verify compliance and would issue later guidance. A contemporaneous National Immigration Law Center analysis explained that a separate PRWORA provision leaves states a choice about offering or restricting WIC; it reported that Idaho alone had chosen to restrict federally funded WIC as of July 2025. This documents a July federal interpretation and a state-specific implementation context. It does not support the frozen entry’s claim that a February 2025 federal order barred lawful immigrants and immigrant families from WIC nationwide. The accessed sources do not establish an automatic federal cutoff for every WIC participant or provide beneficiary-level outcome data. Claims in the old synopsis about U.S.-born children being barred, pediatricians warning about formula denial, or researchers projecting malnutrition and low birth weight are not supported by these sources and are excluded from this corrected copy.
